title: Sustainable electron beam-crosslinked carrageenan/gelatin-pomegranate peel hydrogels for uranyl ions sequestration: mechanistic insights, nonlinear adsorption modelling, and thermodynamics
content: Wastewater from plating facilities, electronic device manufacturing, and nuclear power plants may contain uranium species, which pose serious environmental risks and necessitate the development of effective and sustainable adsorbents. In this study, green composite hydrogels based on carrageenan and gelatin (KC/Gelt), reinforced with pomegranate peel (PP), were successfully fabricated using electron-beam irradiation without the use of chemical crosslinkers. Various analytical techniques were employed to characterize the structural and physicochemical properties of the prepared hydrogels. Batch adsorption experiments were conducted under different conditions, including pH, contact time, initial U(vi) concentration, and adsorbent dosage, to determine the optimum conditions for uranyl ion removal from aqueous solutions. Nonlinear kinetic analysis using the pseudo-first-order (PFO), pseudo-second-order (PSO), Avrami, and intraparticle diffusion models revealed that, based on R2, the fitting order was Avrami ≈ PFO > PSO > intraparticle diffusion for (KC/Gelt)-PP, whereas PSO ≈ Avrami > PFO > intraparticle diffusion was obtained for (KC/Gelt). Based on the reduced chi-square (χ2) values, the fitting order was PFO > PSO > Avrami > intraparticle diffusion for (KC/Gelt)-PP and PSO > Avrami > PFO > intraparticle diffusion for (KC/Gelt). Nonlinear isotherm analysis demonstrated that the Freundlich model provided the best description of the equilibrium adsorption data for both hydrogels, as evidenced by its higher R2 values and lower reduced χ2 values compared with the Langmuir model, indicating the heterogeneous nature of the adsorption surfaces. The Langmuir-derived theoretical adsorption capacities were 185.05 mg g−1 for (KC/Gelt) and 338.82 mg g−1 for (KC/Gelt)-PP, demonstrating the enhanced adsorption capacity achieved through PP incorporation. Thermodynamic analysis further indicated that the adsorption process was spontaneous and feasible under the investigated conditions. These results indicate that the created green hydrogel composites are a promising, environmentally acceptable, and cost-effective solution for removing uranium pollutants from aqueous environments.
